intro: A wall has a site and an audience before an image arrives. Compare marking a place, working with the site and using public images to bring community concerns into view.
alt: Four contemporary studies show interlocked spray-painted shapes, a sidewalk stencil, a photo collage and a Black community arts display.

variants.name: graffiti
variants.look: Large interlocking lines catch the eye against the wall. Look for the soft overspray outside an otherwise firm edge.
variants.history: Modern graffiti writing developed distinctive communities and techniques in cities including Philadelphia and New York, particularly from the late 1960s.
variants.when: Study signatures and letterforms as graphic choices within the contexts that developed them.
variants.why: An outline can remain recognizable even when lettering stretches, overlaps or becomes highly stylized.

source.label: Museum of the City of New York

variants.name: street art
variants.look: A small stencil works with a crack and the surrounding sidewalk to create a single visual moment.
variants.history: Street art spans many public practices, including stencils, pasted images and installations, with overlapping histories and communities with graffiti.
variants.when: Study the setting when a design makes an architectural feature or everyday surface look different.
variants.why: A familiar street detail becomes part of the image, giving it a scale, direction and immediate audience.

variants.name: feminist art
variants.look: Repeated domestic objects and hands invite viewers to read the collage as a question about labor.
variants.history: From the 1960s onward, many feminist artists used pictures, performance, protest and publishing to challenge assumptions about gender and power.
variants.when: Name the question the art asks before studying its imagery or media.
variants.why: Putting an ordinary task into a public image changes who sees the work and who is asked to value it.

variants.name: Black Arts Movement
variants.look: Strong gestures and bright color bring a community ensemble into focus.
variants.history: During the 1960s and 1970s, the Black Arts Movement developed institutions and work across the visual arts, theater, literature, music and other media.
variants.when: Study the image beside the community programs or public gatherings that gave it an audience.
variants.why: A shared place and a familiar visual language can turn an artwork into part of community dialogue.

source.label: Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture
